opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. It's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about almost every day, both on the research side and from what we see with teams building visual AI systems.

The short version is that foundation models are shifting humans from being *producers* of labels to being *curators and verifiers* of data. For a long time the mental model was: you collect a big pile of images or video, you ship it off to an annotation workforce, they draw boxes or polygons on everything, and you train on that. Humans were essentially the label factory.

Now, with strong zero-shot detectors, segmentation models, and vision-language models, you can get a pretty reasonable first pass on a huge fraction of your data almost for free. We've seen in our own experiments that auto-labeling with these models can get you surprisingly close to human-labeled performance on many common tasks, at a tiny fraction of the cost and time. So the question becomes: if the machine can do the bulk of the drawing, what's the human for?

I'd say three things. First, humans define what "correct" means. Ontologies, edge cases, what counts as a pedestrian versus a person on a scooter: that's a judgment call grounded in your application, and a foundation model doesn't know your product requirements. Second, humans find and fix the failures. The models are confidently wrong in systematic ways, on rare classes, unusual viewpoints, domain shift, so the high-value work is surfacing those failure modes and correcting them, not re-labeling the easy ninety percent. Third, humans decide what data matters at all. Selecting, de-duplicating, balancing, finding the long tail: that curation has a huge impact on model performance, often more than squeezing out marginal label quality.

So I don't think the human goes away. I think the human moves up the stack. The annotator becomes much more like a data scientist or a domain expert reviewing and steering the process. And that actually raises the bar on tooling, because you need to be able to visualize your data, understand where the model's labels are uncertain, and focus human attention where it counts. That's really where I think the field is heading: less brute-force labeling, much more thoughtful, human-in-the-loop data work.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models can automatically label a huge fraction of data and handle the bulk of the drawing, with performance close to human labels on many common tasks.

r002.rationale: The response describes humans curating, defining correctness, and reviewing or correcting failures. It does not limit their role to answering questions posed by a labeling agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, both as a researcher and on the Voxel51 side. I think the honest answer is that foundation models are changing the role of humans, but they're not eliminating it, and anyone who tells you otherwise is probably selling something.

Here's how I'd frame it. For a long time, annotation was this very linear, very labor-intensive thing. You've got a pile of images or video, you hand it to a team, they draw boxes, they draw polygons, they type in class labels, and you get back a dataset. And the human was the primary source of every single label. That model is clearly breaking down. With something like SAM, or a CLIP-style model, or a vision-language model, you can get a surprisingly good first pass on a huge fraction of your data with essentially zero human effort. So the question becomes, what do you do with the humans?

And I think the answer is the human moves up the stack. Instead of being the labeler, the human becomes the curator, the auditor, the person who decides what matters. The foundation model gives you a draft, and the human's job is to figure out where that draft is wrong, where it's confidently wrong, which is the dangerous case, and where the data itself is weird or underrepresented or just not the kind of data you thought you had.

So the work shifts from "label everything" to "find the ten percent that actually needs a human." And that's a fundamentally different skill. It's much closer to data science than to clicking on pixels. You need tooling that lets you look at embeddings, look at model uncertainty, look at disagreement between models, and surface the samples where attention is going to pay off. That's a big part of why we built FiftyOne the way we did. The bottleneck is no longer drawing the box. The bottleneck is knowing which box to look at.

There's a second piece too, which is that foundation models reframe what annotation even is. If I've got a model that can do open-vocabulary detection, I don't necessarily need a fixed taxonomy decided up front by a committee. I can be a lot more exploratory. I can ask questions of the dataset. So some of the human role becomes almost like querying and refining, rather than specifying a schema and executing it.

Now, I'd put some caveats on this. The foundation models are great on the kinds of data they've seen a lot of, which is roughly internet imagery. The moment you get into medical imaging, or industrial inspection, or anything where the domain shift is significant, that first pass degrades, sometimes badly, and you're right back to needing expert humans. And in those domains the expert's time is extremely expensive, so being surgical about where you spend it matters even more.

The other caveat is quality. There's a real risk of what I'd call label laundering, where a model produces a label, a human glances at it and accepts it, and now it looks like human ground truth even though nobody really scrutinized it. If you then train on that and evaluate on that, you're grading the model with its own homework. So the human-in-the-loop part has to be designed deliberately, with actual verification, not just rubber-stamping.

So, net-net, I'm optimistic. I think the drudgery goes away, which is good for everybody. But the human judgment piece, deciding what the data should be, what good looks like, where the model is fooling you, that becomes more important, not less. It just looks a lot less like annotation and a lot more like data engineering and data science.

r001.rationale: It says foundation models can produce a good first pass on much of the data with little human effort, shifting human work to the cases that need attention.

r002.rationale: It describes humans as curators, auditors, and people who query and refine datasets, but does not limit their role to answering questions posed by a labeling agent.

astra-6.text:
I think foundation models shift where humans spend their time in the annotation process. Instead of asking someone to draw every bounding box or label every image from scratch, we can have a model propose annotations and have the person correct them, resolve ambiguities, and focus on the cases where the model struggles.

But that doesn’t eliminate the human role. There’s still a fundamental question of what you want the system to recognize. What counts as an event? Where does one action end and another begin? Those are often application-specific decisions, and a foundation model doesn’t automatically know your intent.

So I see annotation becoming more of an interaction. The human provides guidance, the model does more of the repetitive work, and the human checks whether the result actually captures what matters. The challenge is making that interaction efficient without turning the person into someone who just rubber-stamps the model’s predictions.

r001.rationale: The model proposes annotations and handles repetitive work, but the response still assigns humans correction and checking; it does not clearly say models could replace human labeling in many typical cases.

r002.rationale: The response describes humans guiding and checking model annotations, but not a setup where their participation is limited to answering questions posed by a labeling agent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models shift the role of the human rather than eliminate it. Instead of asking someone to label every example from scratch, we can have a model produce an initial annotation and ask the person to correct it, resolve ambiguity, or focus on cases where the model is struggling.

But there’s a distinction between producing a label and knowing that it’s the right label for your problem. The human still has to define what matters. What are the categories? Where are the boundaries between them? What kinds of mistakes are acceptable? Those are often contextual decisions that you can’t just hand off to a model.

So I see annotation becoming more of an interaction: the model does more of the repetitive work, and people provide judgment and feedback. The challenge is making that interaction effective, because reviewing a model’s suggestion can also bias you toward accepting it. We still need ways to check quality and make sure the human is contributing meaningful oversight.

r001.rationale: The response says models can produce initial annotations and handle more repetitive work, but it does not clearly state that they could replace human labeling for many typical cases; it explicitly says they do not eliminate the human role.

r002.rationale: The response describes humans correcting suggestions, resolving ambiguity, defining criteria, and providing oversight. It does not limit human participation to answering questions posed by a labeling agent.
